summary:
The service started this run, not an instruction. It began when the friction-off loop at f* 0.65 at width 200 ended (E0074, job 164667). There were no Asked items, so nothing went unanswered and no time went to unasked work. No claims were proposed or changed, and none are open on this line. The run did three things. (1) It collected the f* 0.65 loop, which completed all 213 steps at 101.0 CPU-hours. (2) It cancelled the seven friction-off loops still running (f* 0.57 to 0.27). Each had used about 101.1 CPU-hours, past the 100 CPU-hour per-run limit in budgets.yaml (decision D0094). (3) It opened blocker B0009, which asks Chris whether to resume them.

The collected numbers reproduce exactly. I reran the committed collector, tools/collect_width200_loops.py, on the mirrored step summaries of all ten loops. All 1,633 per-step entries match evidence/E0074-results.json, including each summary file's SHA-256, with zero mismatches. Every per-loop field matches too. No step of any loop stopped, and there are no energy gains, audit failures or slow stretches. The last completed Gamma of each cancelled loop is as the summary says. The median cost ratio of a matched step, width 200 over width 100, is 9.7 to 11.1 going up and 7.0 to 9.9 going down. The ten job records show 80.5, 89.9 and 101.0 CPU-hours for the three complete loops and 101.13 to 101.15 for the seven cancelled ones, as listed.

The cancellation was the right call, and it can be undone. DIRECTION.md says to stop spending at 100% of a limit until Chris raises it. Every cancelled run folder's manifest (A0204 to A0210) holds the checkpoint of the last completed step and of the step it was cut in. tools/ramp.py resumes a step whose summary has no outcome from its checkpoint, so 'resumable with the same command' holds. The run says plainly that the overrun was foreseeable, and so it was. E0074's own registration priced loops at up to 101 CPU-hours, which DIRECTION.md says needs asking first. My Nov 26 review of this line confirmed that the two loops collected then were each under 100 CPU-hours. But it did not warn that the eight still running would pass the limit at a cost ratio of about ten. I should have; the Nov 24 L0015 review had raised the same risk for that line.

One point overstates, and it is in the question put to Chris. The question and the proposed directions say finishing would take 'about 17 to 173 more CPU-hours each, about 540 in all'. The agent took a whole-loop estimate (the width-100 loop total times the up-leg ratio) and subtracted what had been spent. That estimate already ran 2 to 8% above the real cost of the three completed loops (82, 96 and 109 against 80.5, 89.9 and 101.0), and the error falls entirely on the part still to run. I priced only the steps still to run instead: each remaining width-100 step from evidence/E0060-results.json, times that loop's measured ratio for its leg. That gives about 6, 13, 27, 35, 57, 120 and 144 CPU-hours for f* 0.57, 0.50, 0.44, 0.38, 0.33, 0.30 and 0.27, about 400 in all. Using the up-leg ratio throughout gives about 490. Decision D0094 itself says f* 0.57 had '13 steps left, about 7 hours', which disagrees with the 17 in the question. The proposed direction to resume the four nearest loops ('about 17 to 57 more each') would cost about 6 to 35 by the same reckoning. Totals per finished loop are therefore about 107 to 245, not 118 to 274. This does not change the decision Chris faces: every finished loop would still pass 100 CPU-hours. But the costs Chris is asked to weigh are about a quarter too high. The next run should restate them in B0009's answer or the line's next field, from the remaining steps.

The line state for 'Wider or deeper box' (L0018) says what the evidence says. Both points from my Nov 26 review were answered. The state now says the width-100 nudge loop at f* 0.30 ended still climbing at 4.3, and that at f* 0.30 width 200 shows no cost rise by Gamma 4.4 (162 and 161 CPU-seconds a cycle). The earlier summary's headline cannot be edited, as the run notes. 'A step costs about 10 times the width-100 step' is a little round for the down legs (7 to 10 times), but the summary gives the range. The pinned table lines/L0018/pinned/working-ranges.md agrees with the evidence file row for row.

program check passes (once my own scratch folder was removed). It reports 820.6 of 10,000 weekly CPU-hours, still an undercount. The eight jobs collected here total 809 CPU-hours by their job records, so the week is about 2,500 (about 25%), as the summary says. The latest approval is still approved/20261124T031934297997Z (Nov 24), so none were made in the last day. sequel-data is 696 megabytes against a 15 gigabyte ceiling, and free disk is 81 gigabytes against a 40 gigabyte floor. sequel-data/tmp/ is empty, and active.jsonl is empty. Outside the two allowed folders, the only writes since the run began are the harness's own. As the user instructed, this review is committed on branch line/L0018 in the line's worktree.

run_conditions.assessment: This was an eight-minute service run, from 11:20:13 to 11:28:32 (commit at 11:29:51). It collected one ended loop and recorded seven cancelled ones as artifacts with job records. It wrote one results file for all ten loops and updated the pinned table, the line records, a decision and a blocker. It started no jobs. Nothing is left running for this line: all thirty width-200 loops have ended. What waits is Chris's answer on B0009 and the line's registered test, where the pattern appears, which has not been measured at either width. The host is a Linux container, so pmset and uptime are unavailable, as the summary says. The load average (/proc/loadavg) now is 1.1 to 2.3, which fits its 3.0 at the start. Free disk of 81 gigabytes matches. The machine did not limit the science. The program's per-run CPU limit did: seven friction-off loops stopped short of their down legs.
discrepancies: evidence/E0074-results.json gives made_at 2026-11-26T11:45:00Z. That is after the run ended (11:28:32) and after its commit (11:29:51), so the timestamp was not measured.

D0094 says the jobs were cancelled 'about 11:24Z'. The Slurm elapsed times (4-05:08 from about 06:13Z on Nov 22) and the artifact records (A0204 at 11:23:06) put the cancellations at about 11:22. This is a minor point.
budget.cpu_hours_week.spent is program check's undercount of 820.6. The summary's limits_hit text gives the true figure, about 2,500, which matches my count.

The interrupted step of each cancelled loop is listed with 0.0 CPU-hours so far. That is ramp.py's placeholder summary, not a measurement. The job records exceed the sum of completed steps by 0.87 to 1.44 CPU-hours, against 0.86 to 0.93 for complete loops. So each cut step had used at most about half an hour, the most at f* 0.33.
